meta.note: Hand-written hero blurbs (why_it_matters) keyed by plant id, plus manual Canadian records. Blurb claims are ledgered in content/grid/facts.md and audited in Phase 5. Canadian capacities/coordinates are approximate and PROVISIONAL.

blurbs.eia-649: Units 3 and 4 are the first American reactors built from scratch in a generation — roughly $35 billion and fourteen years in the making — and they made Vogtle the largest nuclear plant in the country.
blurbs.eia-6008: For nearly forty years the largest nuclear plant in America, dethroned only by Vogtle's new units — and still the only big plant in the country not sited on a body of water. It cools itself with Phoenix's treated sewage.
blurbs.eia-6103: The 4 a.m. hum of Act Two. Since 2024 its operator has been wiring the plant directly to data-center campuses next door — the AI buildout shaking hands with the 1983 grid.
blurbs.eia-6099: California's last nuclear plant, scheduled to close and reprieved by the state legislature when the math on replacing it stopped working.
blurbs.eia-46: TVA's giant on the Tennessee River, and the plant whose 1975 fire — started by a worker checking for air leaks with a candle — rewrote American nuclear safety rules.
blurbs.eia-6251: Among the most efficient plants of the old build-out era. It froze anyway in Uri when one exposed sensing line iced over — one small pipe, one reactor offline.
blurbs.eia-3166: Boiling-water reactors running since 1974, on a site that hosted an experimental helium-cooled reactor a decade before that. The industry's whole arc inside one fence line.
blurbs.eia-3265: Duke's three-reactor workhorse, and one of the first US plants licensed to run for eighty years — the opening bet of the fleet-life-extension era.
blurbs.eia-6145: One of ERCOT's two nuclear stations. With the grid an island, these reactors are Texas's bedrock supply — they held through Uri while gas froze around them.
blurbs.eia-6163: The largest power plant in America of any kind — 6,800 megawatts of Columbia River — and the machine that powered the aluminum for a bomber a day in the 1940s.
blurbs.eia-154: The dam that electrified the Southwest and named an era. It appears on this map twice: Nevada and Arizona split the powerhouse down the state line.
blurbs.eia-8902: The Arizona half of Hoover's powerhouse. The state line runs through the dam.
blurbs.eia-2693: New York's biggest generator, drinking the Niagara River at night when the tourists aren't looking — by treaty, the falls get their water back at showtime.
blurbs.eia-6167: America's biggest battery by far, and it was built in 1985: two reservoirs a quarter-mile apart in elevation that swallow and return a city's worth of power every day.
blurbs.eia-1713: Michigan's water battery on a Lake Michigan bluff — pump-turbines that drink the lake overnight and pour it back through the morning ramp.
blurbs.eia-6151: TVA hollowed out a mountaintop and made it a battery: the summit reservoir holds roughly a day of full output for Chattanooga's grid.
blurbs.eia-3470: One of the country's largest fossil plants, coal and gas side by side southwest of Houston — and host of Petra Nova, the flagship American attempt at capturing carbon from coal.
blurbs.eia-6257: For years the largest coal plant in America and its single biggest carbon source. Its slow, partial wind-down is the national coal story in one site.
blurbs.eia-6076: The coal plant the Western grid was partly built around — wired five hundred miles to Seattle and Portland, whose owners now disagree about when to let it die.
blurbs.eia-56407: One of the largest gas plants in America, built in three matched blocks as Florida bet its grid almost entirely on gas.
blurbs.eia-60357: Act One's anchor: 1,500 megawatts built on the site logic of the shale era — directly on top of the Marcellus gas that feeds it.
blurbs.eia-56291: The wind farm that announced the Texas wind boom — briefly the largest on earth in 2006, now one turbine field among hundreds on the same plains.
blurbs.eia-63479: Nearly a gigawatt in a single Oklahoma project — the largest single-phase wind farm in North America when it spun up in 2022.
blurbs.eia-57282: One phase of the Alta complex in the Tehachapi Pass — a dozen projects that together form America's largest wind cluster, feeding Los Angeles on dedicated lines.
blurbs.eia-58388: With its twin next door, the largest photovoltaic plant on earth at its 2015 ribbon-cutting. The record has fallen many times since — which is the point of the solar era.
blurbs.eia-57695: One of the first giant solar farms financed like infrastructure instead of an experiment — Warren Buffett's utility bought it before construction finished.
blurbs.eia-57993: Twin blocks in the Mojave that, with Topaz, proved the utility-scale solar template: flat desert, big wires, long contracts.
blurbs.eia-63352: Solar plus a giant battery on one plug — panels by day, storage for Las Vegas after dark. The template for most of what waits in the queue.
blurbs.eia-58915: Part of the Copper Mountain complex outside Boulder City — a decade of phases stacked into one of the densest solar zones in the country, next door to Hoover's wires.
blurbs.eia-66494: Act Two's battery: 680 megawatts outside Los Angeles, charged at noon and sold at seven. Among the largest standalone batteries on earth — a category ten years old.
blurbs.eia-65140: A battery in the desert with no plant attached — pure arbitrage on the duck curve, sited on old federal solar land near the Colorado River.
blurbs.eia-286: The Geysers is the largest geothermal complex on earth, generating north of San Francisco since 1960 — and recharged, since the 1990s, with the Bay Area's treated wastewater.

canada.name: Robert-Bourassa
canada.why: The anchor of Hydro-Québec's La Grande complex and the largest underground powerhouse on earth, carved deep into Canadian Shield granite. The arcs on this map running toward New England start here.

canada.name: Manic-5
canada.why: Behind it stands the Daniel-Johnson Dam, the largest multiple-arch buttress dam ever built — a cathedral of 1960s engineering that made Hydro-Québec a national project.

canada.name: Churchill Falls
canada.why: The second-largest underground powerhouse on earth, and the sorest deal in Canadian energy: a 1969 contract sold its output to Hydro-Québec at fixed prices for sixty-five years.

canada.name: Bruce Nuclear Generating Station
canada.why: The largest operating nuclear station in the world — eight reactors on Lake Huron carrying roughly a third of Ontario.

canada.name: Sir Adam Beck I & II
canada.why: Niagara's Canadian side, generating since 1922. With Robert Moses across the river, it splits the falls' allowance under the same treaty.

canada.name: G.M. Shrum (W.A.C. Bennett Dam)
canada.why: Ten units behind the W.A.C. Bennett Dam, holding back a reservoir the size of a small sea — the plant that made BC Hydro a trading power in the US West.

canada.name: Limestone
canada.why: The biggest of Manitoba Hydro's Nelson River chain, sending sub-Arctic water south over HVDC lines into the middle of the American grid.

canada.name: Travers Solar
canada.why: Canada's largest solar farm, built merchant in Alberta's energy-only market — the AESO, ERCOT's small northern cousin.
